pages.name: Inside the diode
pages.text: A diode is a one-way valve for current. Here is one way to see why. Inside is one piece of silicon, treated so its two halves differ. The N side has spare free electrons. The P side is short of electrons. Each gap is a [[hole]], and it acts like a positive charge. Where the halves meet, electrons cross and fill holes. That leaves a thin empty zone with no free carriers. It also leaves charge behind, minus on the P side and plus on the N side.

pages.name: Why the crossing stops
pages.task: Why does the crossing stop, leaving most holes and electrons where they were?
pages.answer: The charge left behind pushes the next carriers back
pages.why: Each electron that crosses leaves a plus behind on the N side and a minus on the P side. That charge pushes back on the next electrons and holes. The crossing stops once that push balances their spreading.

pages.name: Across the diode
pages.task: The supply is at 5 V and the diode conducts 0.43 A. What does a voltmeter across the diode read?
pages.why: Carriers stream across only while the zone is held thin. That takes about 0.7 V. The other 4.30 V of the 5 V sits across the resistor and drives 0.43 A.

pages.name: Reverse
pages.text: At −20 V the zone is wide. Almost no current flows, and the diode holds all 20 V. At −60 V, past the 50 V PIV, the diode has broken down. It holds 50 V while 1.00 A flows backwards. So it turns 50 W into heat, shown in red.

pages.name: A test record
pages.task: A test record says a silicon diode carried 0.5 A forward with 0.1 V across it. Can that be right?
pages.answer: No: at 0.1 V the curve gives almost no current
pages.why: At 0.1 V the zone is still wide enough to hold the carriers back. So the curve sits on zero. 0.5 A needs about 0.7 V. So the record is wrong, or the part is not a working diode.
options: Yes: forward, a diode is a closed switch
Yes: more current means less drop

pages.name: Nothing used up
pages.text: Put an ammeter each side of the diode. Both read 0.43 A. Current is a flow of charge. Charge is not used up on the way through. What the diode takes is voltage, about 0.7 V of push. It turns that into heat at voltage × current. That is the P = V × I you already use. Here that is 0.70 × 0.43 = 0.30 W. The drop barely changes with current. So the heat grows almost in step with the current.

pages.task: Now the supply is at 10 V. The ammeter before the diode reads 0.93 A. What does the one after it read?
pages.why: Every bit of charge that enters the diode leaves the other end. The diode takes 0.72 V of push. It turns that into 0.72 × 0.93 = 0.67 W of heat. All 0.93 A flows on to the resistor.

pages.name: Good or not?
pages.task: A meter on its diode range reads 0.55 V across a silicon diode one way, and over range the other way. Is the diode good?
pages.answer: Yes: a drop one way, blocking the other
pages.why: The meter pushes only a tiny current. So a good silicon diode typically reads under 0.7 V. Over range the other way means it blocks. A drop one way and a block the other is a good diode.

pages.name: Where the 20 V sit
pages.task: The supply is set to −20 V, well inside the diode's 50 V PIV. Where do the 20 V sit?
pages.why: The wide zone lets almost no current through. With almost no current, the resistor drops almost nothing. So the diode holds the whole supply. That is why its PIV must be above it.

pages.name: Heat in a charger
pages.task: A silicon diode in a battery charger carries 20 A with about 0.7 V across it. How much heat does it make?
pages.why: Heat = voltage × current = 0.7 × 20 = 14 W. A real diode's drop creeps up at high current, as the curve does. So it makes more.
